issues: Significance claimed the ruling came 'decades before the first data-protection statutes'. The first data-protection statute (Hesse) dates from 1970, only six years later. 'Decades' holds only for Japan's own general law, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information of 2003, which the same JILPT paper cites.

Significance also said the ruling undercut 'the idea that privacy law is a purely Western export', but the record's own summary and source say Japan adopted the American 'right to be let alone' after scholars imported it (the paper cites Masami Ito, 1963). The ruling shows a US idea adopted and made enforceable in Japan, not a home-grown alternative. Reworded.

All other claims check out. The date 28 September 1964 and the citation 15-9 Kaminshu 2317 are in the source. Japanese case-law summaries independently give 東京地判昭和39年9月28日 and name the plaintiff as 有田八郎 (Hachiro Arita), and they describe the right protected as 私生活をみだりに公開されない権利 ('the right not to have one's private life disclosed without good reason'). 'Early 1960s' fits the Ito (1963) footnote. The coordinates match the Tokyo District Court at Kasumigaseki 1-1-4.

fieldFixes.significance: Shows a court outside Europe and the United States taking up the American idea of privacy and making it an enforceable right in 1964, six years before the first data-protection statute (Hesse, 1970) and nearly four decades before Japan's general Act on the Protection of Personal Information (2003).

fieldFixes.summary: Israel's Protection of Privacy Law, 5741-1981, made infringement of privacy both a civil wrong and, in its wilful forms, a criminal offence, and added rules for registering and running databases. Enacted soon after the OECD's 1980 Privacy Guidelines, it was one of the world's first attempts at a comprehensive statutory privacy framework. It was overhauled by Amendment 13, approved on 5 August 2024 and in force from 14 August 2025.
fieldFixes.significance: An early non-European omnibus law that later won Israel an EU adequacy finding, and one that puts a general privacy right, a privacy tort and database regulation in a single statute.

issues: The summary says the reform 'added to Article 43' a right, which implies Article 43 already existed. In fact Article 43 as a whole (amparo, with habeas data in its third paragraph) was new in 1994. It sits in the chapter 'Nuevos derechos y garantías' (arts. 36 to 43) that the reform created.

Significance overstated Argentina's role. The habeas data model had already spread from Brazil to Colombia (1991 Constitution, Art. 15, which covers 'public and private entities'), Paraguay (1992, Art. 135 'Del habeas data', which covers 'official or private registries of a public character') and Peru (1993, Art. 200(3)). So Argentina neither 'carried the habeas data model ... across Latin America' nor was first to extend it to private databanks.

Source 0 date: the cited page is the Ley 24.430 official-text publication (Boletín Oficial 10-01-1995), not a 22 August 1994 document. The constitutional text it reproduces is dated 22 August 1994 in Santa Fe.

Confirmed: the text of the third paragraph of Art. 43 (including 'supresión, rectificación, confidencialidad o actualización' in case of 'falsedad o discriminación'); 'DADA ... EN LA CIUDAD DE SANTA FE, A LOS VEINTIDÓS DÍAS DEL MES DE AGOSTO ... 1994'; the Convention sitting in Santa Fe and Paraná (Ley 24.430 art. 2); and recital 7 of Decision 2003/490/EC calling habeas data a fundamental right.

fieldFixes.summary: The 1994 reform of Argentina's constitution, sanctioned by the Constituent Convention in the city of Santa Fe on 22 August 1994, added a new Article 43 whose third paragraph gives every person a habeas data action: the right to learn what data about them is held in public registers or in private databanks that supply reports, and to demand its deletion, correction, confidentiality or updating where it is false or discriminatory. The European Commission later described this habeas data remedy as making data protection a fundamental right in Argentina.
fieldFixes.significance: Joined the wave of new Latin American constitutions that took up Brazil's habeas data (Colombia 1991, Paraguay 1992, Peru 1993). Like Colombia's and Paraguay's, it reached private databanks, and it became the foundation on which Argentina built its 2000 data-protection law.

fieldFixes.title: Chile enacts Latin America's first general data-protection statute
fieldFixes.summary: Law No. 19.628 on the protection of private life, published in the Diario Oficial on 28 August 1999, regulated the processing of personal data in registers and databanks held by public bodies and private parties. It created no supervisory authority, so people had to go to the ordinary courts to enforce it. Law 21.719, published on 13 December 2024, rewrote it and created a Personal Data Protection Agency; the new regime takes full effect in December 2026.
fieldFixes.significance: Began the shift in Latin America from constitutional habeas data to general statutes, though for a quarter of a century Chile's law had no regulator to enforce it.

fieldFixes.title: Cabo Verde enacts Africa's first data-protection law
fieldFixes.summary: Law No. 133/V/2001, approved by the National Assembly on 20 December 2000 and dated 22 January 2001, made Cabo Verde the first African country to enact comprehensive data-protection legislation. It closely followed European law, as Cabo Verde's legal system draws on Portugal's, and it put into effect Article 44 of the Constitution, which already gave citizens the right of access to computerised data about them and to have it corrected. Amended in 2013 and 2021, the law was later backed by a national data-protection commission (CNPD).

issues: Legal basis misstated. The summary says the Commission 'decided under Article 25(2)'. The decision was adopted under Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC ('in particular Article 25(6) thereof'). Article 1 finds Argentina adequate 'for the purposes of Article 25(2)', which is the provision listing the factors for assessing adequacy.

Place is anachronistic. The Commission was out of the Berlaymont from 1991 to 2004 for asbestos removal and renovation, and was based in the Breydel building (Wikipedia: 'temporary headquarters for the European Commission between 1991 and 2004'). The decision says only 'Done at Brussels'. Place and coordinates changed to the Breydel building (50.8400, 4.3850).

Significance overclaims. Argentina did not first 'show' that a non-European country could gain access to European data flows: Canada's adequacy decision (2002/2/EC, 20 December 2001) came earlier. 'Buy access' is loaded wording. Reworded.
